title: Recovery-oriented practice and harm reduction
summary: A stance that shapes goals and plan wording: recovery as a personal journey toward a meaningful life (connection, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment), and harm reduction as meeting people where they are and supporting any positive change, including with substance use.
whenToUse: When writing goals and plans with people living with long-term or recurring mental health or substance use problems.
When a client does not want, or is not ready for, abstinence or symptom elimination.
When services have felt coercive or stigmatizing to the client.

steps.heading: Start from the person's own goals
steps.body: Ask what a good life would look like for them, beyond symptoms. Write goals in their words, about the life they want.

steps.heading: Use the recovery dimensions
items: Hope: belief that things can improve, and stories of others who have.
Identity: a sense of self beyond illness or substance use.
Meaning: valued roles, work, faith, creativity.
Empowerment: choice, control, and building on strengths.

steps.heading: Support any positive change
steps.body: In harm reduction, any reduction in harm counts: using less, using more safely, fewer risky situations, or more contact with care. Abstinence is one goal among several, not a condition of care.

steps.heading: Offer practical safety
items: Overdose education and naloxone where opioids or other substances may be involved.
Safer-use information from trusted public health sources.
Links to medicine for opioid or alcohol use, mutual help and peer support, as the client wishes.

steps.heading: Watch the language
steps.body: Use person-first or the person's own words. Avoid labels such as addict, abuser or non-compliant in notes and plans.

prompts: If things were going well in your life a year from now, what would you be doing?
You do not want to stop completely right now. What changes would make things safer or better for you, even a little?
Who in your life, or what kind of support, helps you feel more like yourself?
Would it be useful to talk about how to stay safer if you do use, including what to do in an overdose?
cautions: Harm reduction is not an absence of concern; continue to talk about risks, including overdose and withdrawal, honestly.
Alcohol and sedative withdrawal can be dangerous; any plan to stop suddenly needs medical advice.
Records that include substance-use information may be protected by 42 CFR Part 2; follow consent rules before sharing.
Recovery language should never be used to deny people care or to blame them for setbacks.

adaptations.adaptation: Combine recovery goals with practical support (housing, work, benefits) and peer support, and plan for early warning signs.
Start with immediate needs and safety; therapy goals can follow once basic needs are being met.

evidenceSummary: A 2011 systematic review (Leamy and colleagues) identified the CHIME framework of personal recovery: connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment. A 2014 review (Slade and colleagues) describes uses and misuses of recovery in services. A 2017 paper (Hawk and colleagues) sets out harm reduction principles for healthcare settings. WHO guidance (2021) promotes person-centred, recovery-oriented and rights-based community mental health services.
